items.text: You must be 19 or older to buy, use, possess or grow recreational cannabis. Adults may carry up to 30 g of dried cannabis (or equivalent) in public. Smoking or vaping is allowed in private residences, many outdoor public places and designated hotel rooms, but not in enclosed public places or workplaces, or near schools, playgrounds, child care and hospitals. Buy only from the Ontario Cannabis Store or authorised stores.

laws.rule: The legal age for cannabis in Ontario is 19. Adults may carry up to 30 g of dried cannabis (or equivalent) in public, and buy only from private licensed stores or the government online store.

Toronto's Alcohol in Parks Program lets people aged 19 and over bring and drink their own alcohol in the listed City parks only, during park hours (5:30 am to midnight). Drinking is not allowed within 2 metres of playgrounds, wading pools, splash pads, outdoor pools, outdoor ice rinks and skateboard or BMX parks, and nothing may be supplied to under-19s. The City's page lists 55 parks while its own background section refers to 45 parks adopted in April 2024, so check the current list. Selling or serving alcohol in a park needs a City Special Event permit and an Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario permit. Drinking in a park that is not on the list is an offence under the City's parks bylaw.
laws.penalty_signal: parks bylaw fines range from C$100 to C$750 (about A$102 to A$762 at A$1 = C$0.9838, RBA 30 Oct 2026)

laws.rule: In Toronto parks you cannot smoke or vape (cannabis included) within 20 metres of listed areas such as playgrounds and sports fields. Lighting or stoking an open fire or bonfire in a park needs a permit, and so does parking a vehicle overnight.

Smoking or holding lit cannabis, smoking tobacco and using an e-cigarette are banned in enclosed public places and workplaces, schools and school grounds, indoor common areas of apartment buildings, child care centres, and the reserved seating areas of sports arenas (Smoke-Free Ontario Act, 2017, s. 12(1) and (2)). Regulation 268/18 adds restaurant and bar patios and public areas within 9 metres of their edge (s. 7), children's playgrounds and public areas within 20 metres of them, public areas within 20 metres of sporting areas and their spectator areas, and the outdoor grounds of hospitals plus 9 metres around entrances. Cannabis smoking is otherwise allowed wherever tobacco smoking is.

Nobody may consume cannabis in any form in a vehicle or boat that is being driven or is under someone's care or control, and that includes passengers, whether or not it is moving (Smoke-Free Ontario Act, 2017, s. 17.1). Under the Cannabis Control Act, 2017, s. 12, cannabis in a vehicle or boat must be in its original unopened packaging or packed in closed baggage that is not readily available to anyone in the vehicle. Police may search without a warrant if they suspect a breach. Under-19s may not possess, buy or consume cannabis (s. 10), and sellers must check ID if the buyer looks under 25 (s. 7).

Under the Liquor Licence Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.19, s. 31(2), liquor may be had or drunk only in a residence (a tent and the land next to it counts), licensed premises, a private place as defined in the regulations, or a public place a municipal council has designated by by-law. Liquor in a closed container is exempt (s. 31(3)). Being intoxicated in a place open to the public is an offence and police may arrest if needed for safety (s. 31(4) and (5)).

The legal drinking age is 19. Nobody under 19 may have, drink, try to buy or buy liquor, and selling or supplying it to someone who appears under 19 is an offence (s. 30(1), (2), (8)). A parent or lawful guardian may supply liquor to a minor in a residence or private place (s. 30).

Open liquor in a motor vehicle or snowmobile is banned, moving or not, unless it is in a container with the seal unbroken or packed in closed baggage not readily available to anyone in the vehicle (s. 32(1) and (2)). Boats that are underway have the same rule, with an alternative of storing liquor in a closed compartment (s. 32(3) and (4)). Police may search without a warrant if they have reasonable grounds.

In Ontario provincial parks a fire may only be lit or tended in a fireplace the superintendent provides or an area designated for it (O. Reg. 347/07, s. 5(1)). Fires are banned where a fire-hazard notice is posted (s. 5(2)). A fire must not be left without a responsible person in charge, and must be extinguished before leaving (s. 5(2.1) and (2.2)). Possessing or igniting fireworks in a provincial park is banned (s. 5(3)). Officers can remove a person for breaching the park rules or the liquor Act in a park (s. 10).

Art Gallery of Ontario: Remain behind stanchions and at a safe, non-touching distance from art. Keep cameras at least 18 inches (about 46 cm) from artworks and never above them. Avoid disrupting access or other visitors.

Art Gallery of Ontario: Personal non-commercial handheld photos without flash, except posted no-photo restrictions. No tripods, monopods, gimbals or selfie sticks. Photographing children requires consent of the accompanying adult. Staged shoots are not permitted during visitor hours, including amateur shoots; ask AGO Events about outside-hours arrangements. Live streaming is allowed only in permanent-collection galleries under the same conditions. Unrelated films/student projects are not accommodated.

layers.process: Backcountry (interior) camping needs a reservation for paddling and backpacking, up to five months ahead, at reservations.ontarioparks.ca or 1-888-668-7275. Paddling: reserve a lake or zone per night; sites in it are first come. Backpacking: reserve a specific site per night. No permit pick-up; keep the reservation letter. Backcountry closes from 1 April until conditions allow. Fees on the 2026 backcountry fees page.

Provincial parks charge a daily vehicle permit for day use, set per park in four levels (2026-27, HST included): regular adult vehicle CAD 12.25 to CAD 21.00 (about A$12.45 to A$21.35 (A$1 = CAD 0.9838, RBA 30 Oct 2026)). Discounts for seniors, people with disabilities and veterans are for Ontario residents only. Most parks let you reserve a daily vehicle permit online up to five days ahead at no extra charge; the pages do not say which parks. Walk-in fees are per person at French River and North Beach.

layers.authority: Parks Canada, Bruce Peninsula National Park
layers.process: Parking at the Grotto and Cyprus Lake area must be reserved from 1 May to 31 October (six 4-hour slots, 8 am to 9 pm). Halfway Log Dump must be reserved from 19 June to 7 September (two 6-hour slots); outside those dates it is first come first served. Little Cove (4-hour slots, 15 May to 15 September) is booked through the Municipality of Northern Bruce Peninsula. Cost is admission (adult CAD 10.00, about A$10.16) plus parking (CAD 17.50 a vehicle, about A$17.79) plus a reservation fee (CAD 3.50 online, about A$3.56; CAD 5.50 by phone, about A$5.59) (A$1 = CAD 0.9838, RBA 30 Oct 2026). The park says it does not recommend travelling without a confirmed reservation; when lots are full there is no other access, and drop-offs are not permitted. Changes are not allowed: cancel and rebook. Phone 1-877-737-3783.
